  • The climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

In a recent development, no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

The climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

In a recent development, vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:.

Sources indicate that we know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt quickly to new conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

The new snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:.

Industry observers note that it is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

According to recent reports, on Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

Ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

Sources indicate that so far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

#44868. Fresh Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Fresh Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (620 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding fresh route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border.
  • Sources indicate that the pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif.
  • Industry observers note that they placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding fresh route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

Sources indicate that the pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

Industry observers note that they placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health issues. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

The fresh line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

In the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Industry observers note that attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

They returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

Industry observers note that in late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

It has been revealed that this was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River.
  • In a recent development, this won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river.
  • According to recent reports, bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

In a recent development, this won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

According to recent reports, bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram.

Bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

Recent findings suggest that though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

But according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this notable riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

The logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

Why I’m Walking Away From Nursing

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I work as a registered nurse, and starting in January, I’ll be trading in my scrubs for trail runners and a backpack.
  • Exchanging vows on the summit of Mount Bierstadt (14,065 feet).
  • Industry observers note that ​Nursing has this way of showing you just how fragile life really is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

​I’m Cat. I work as a registered nurse, and starting in January, I’ll be trading in my scrubs for trail runners and a backpack. My husband and I are known to be spontaneous and challenge ourselves when life starts feeling boring. Packing a U-Haul with whatever fits and moving to a state we’ve never been to, hiking to the top of a mountain in Colorado to exchange vows, buying a house 14 hours away we’ve only seen pictures of online; you could say we live for the spontaneity of life. My motivation for hiking the trail goes far beyond last-minute decision-making; it comes from more recent experiences while working as a nurse.

Exchanging vows on the summit of Mount Bierstadt (14,065 feet).

Industry observers note that ​Nursing has this way of showing you just how fragile life really is. Having worked as a float tech in all units of the hospital and recently as a nurse in ICU step-down and rehab, I’ve cared for adults, both young and old, who lost their health and independence in an instant. I quickly realized I’ve been taking my own health for granted. I didn’t quite know I was in search of a challenge in life, but as always, my husband was at the driver’s seat of a new adventure. This time, it was all on me.

According to recent reports, ​It all started sitting by the fire in our backyard. My seasoned thru-hiker husband asked if I wanted to hike the Appalachian Trail; I shrugged and said okay. A week later, he suggested adding the Florida Trail first to get my trail legs ready; I quickly agreed to that, too. By the third week, he suggested I hike the entire ECT. Just like that, a casual backyard fire turned into a 4,500-mile hike.

Sources indicate that ​I’ll be hiking the Eastern Continental Trail (ECT), which is a connection of trails spanning from Florida to Canada. I decided to blog my adventures to have something to look back on and to share my travels with friends and family. I don’t know what lies ahead of me, but what I do know is I’m about to make so many memories, connections, and mistakes!

If you’d like to follow along with the journey, I’ll be sharing updates, photos, and stories right here while I head north.

It has been revealed that ​The very basic core of a man’s living spirit is his passion for adventure. The joy of life comes from our encounters with new experiences, and hence there is no greater joy than to have an endlessly changing horizon, for each day to have a new and different sun.

—Chris McCandless (​Alexander Supertramp).

Hey, I'm Cat! I've been working as a registered nurse for the last couple of years, but before that, I was a pastry chef turned correctional officer turned dental assistant. You could say I embrace change and enjoy a challenge! My husband and I lived in Colorado for six years, which is where I found my true love for the outdoors. We eloped on one of Colorado's many fourteeners with our two dogs, and since then, it has been one adventure after another. My husband, a seasoned thru-hiker, has encouraged me to embark on my own thru-hiking journey. After logging hundreds of miles in Colorado's wilderness, I completed the Foothills Trail in November 2026 as a shakedown for my upcoming trails. 📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route.
  • The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023.
  • Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Blueprint B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team remarked that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”.

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza.

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

Recent findings suggest that “We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”.

One of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza.

According to recent reports, the Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

Recent findings suggest that the situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

In a recent development, one of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet.

Industry observers note that there was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

It has been revealed that nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet.

Industry observers note that “We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”.

The two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet.

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”.

Industry observers note that otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza remarked.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

“Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”.

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

The recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

In a recent development, satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

Ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung said he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

It has been revealed that on Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

Industry observers note that tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who proposal to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:.

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change promptly.

The route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#44863. Te Araroa day 20: Catching up with friendly faces

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2136 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa day 20: Catching up with friendly faces

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2136 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After my day off the previous day, I was keen to get walking.
  • According to recent reports, the tide was pretty much all the way in, so I had to walk on soft sand which was pretty annoying.
  • According to recent reports, somewhat perturbed but with not much I could do about it, I continued along the beach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

26km, Ruakākā Motor Camp to Waorahi Campsite.

After my day off the previous day, I was keen to get walking. The weather was thankfully looking better – the threat of a few showers, perhaps, but nowhere near as bad as the day before. Feeling energetic, I thought I might end up doing a bigger day and pushing all the way through to Mangawhai Heads, 39km away. Alternatively, I could stay at a free campsite in 26 kilometres. I set out at my usual not-especially-early time, and headed to the beach. The day would start with 5km of beach walking before heading inland.

According to recent reports, the tide was pretty much all the way in, so I had to walk on soft sand which was pretty annoying. As I walked, I kept getting whiffs of pee. I couldn’t work out where it was coming from, but eventually realised that my right hand smelled of pee and traced the smell back to the strap of my hiking pole. And then I realised what must have happened. You see, one of the great but not often discussed advantages of the Durston X-Mid tent is that the vestibule is large enough to squat and pee in. On a rainy night when you just don’t want to leave your tent, that can be a great advantage. And so it had gone the previous night. I had spent the day drinking fruit juice, eating grapes, and chugging water. I’m sure this was great for my hydration, but it meant that I needed to pee in the night, and it was raining. Presumably, the strap of my hiking pole got caught in the cross-fire and ended up with pee on it. And now it was on my hand. Excellent.

According to recent reports, somewhat perturbed but with not much I could do about it, I continued along the beach. Far in the distance, I could see some little figures that looked like hikers. I couldn’t figure out who they could be though, as there were only two and the hiker trio I had been with the day before would have been unlikely to split up so soon. I continued along my way, and gradually got closer – I’m a pretty speedy walker, and my curiosity motivated me to walk rapidly. As I neared them, I started to recognise one of the figures. It looked like they were wearing Annabel’s distinctive flowy shorts, and once I figured that out I was almost certain that one of them was Annabel. And the other person looked like Lindsay to me. Now it made sense – I had kind of forgotten that these two, and a number of others who I had previously been hiking with, had got an AirBnB in Ruakākā for a day off. I would have joined them had I known that I would also be taking a zero the previous day, but since that wasn’t my blueprint, I had stayed at the campground.

Annabel and Lindsay in the distance – this was when I recognised them, although they were more distinct in real life.

Beach walking with Lindsay and Annabel – photo by Sinéad.

In a recent development, happy to see some friends, I put the boosters on and caught up to them fairly promptly. We soon also caught Sinéad, who had been taking a dip in the sea. I explained my ‘pee stick’ problem and we had a good laugh about it. The others threatened to make Pee Sticks my trail name, but I vetoed that pretty quickly! As we were standing around, a man came jogging barefoot down the beach towards us. He stopped by us, asked the now-familiar question (‘are you doing that substantial walk?’) and asked why we didn’t go barefoot on the beach. We told him that our feet needed more support for long kilometres of beach walking, especially with weight on our backs. He looked unconvinced, but wished us luck and jogged away. To be fair, he could probably walk the length of 90 Mile beach without shoes. But I certainly couldn’t!

Sources indicate that it was good to catch up with the others about their day off, and I was having a great time walking with friends again. I realised that I was not going to go all the way to Mangawhai Heads that day – I would much rather hang out with this lot and have a fun time. We had all heard through the grapevine that there was a cafe in Waipu that gave hikers free coffee, so that was our destination for the morning. After the beach, there was a bit of gravel road and then a kilometre or two of main road to walk down to reach Waipu. I was walking with Sinéad and we were chatting away. At one point I looked behind and the others weren’t there. Had we really walked that fast? ‘They probably hitched,’ said Sinéad. Aha. I had forgotten that hitching was a thing – it would never have occurred to me on this short of a road section! But fair enough, there’s no need to walk on busy main roads if you don’t want to.

Sources indicate that we got into Waipu, which was surprisingly popping for a small place on a random Wednesday. I made a beeline for the public toilets to wash the pee smell off my hand and gear, then headed to Logan McClean cafe where legend has it, hikers get a free hot drink. The others were already there, along with the hiker trio from my day off. The lady at the counter at the cafe asked if I was walking too, which saved me from the awkwardness of having to say ‘Sooo, I heard you do free drinks for hikers?’ In addition to my coffee, I got a couple of slices. I couldn’t choose and figured I would take one away with me. We sat outside the cafe for a bit, and Sven turned up too. He hadn’t heard that there was free coffee here, so had bought one at another cafe. But then of course he had to make use of the freebie so got another! A few people came up to talk to us, including an older guy who had done the TA a few years ago. The others had various things to buy at the Four Square and the pharmacy, and then we were back on our way.

Apricot crumble and ginger macadamia slices – I thought I would take one of them away. That didn’t happen, shocker.

The next section looked to be mostly road walking. Sven (ever the hitching fan) and Lindsay hopped in a car, but me, Annabel and Sinéad decided to give the road a go. I wasn’t keen to hitch at all, as this would already be a shorter day for me and I was full of energy from my day off. Things started out promisingly, with a pavement to walk on through the rest of the town. But soon, the pavement stopped and it looked as though we would be on tarmac. Then I happened to glance across the road and saw a TA sign leading to a bike path. Great! The bike path turned out to be reasonably scenic, and we were happy we chose to walk.

At one point, I had to stop to change my sock. I had washed the sand out of my shoes and socks from the end of the last day, but with the rain they hadn’t had a chance to dry. This morning, I had wanted a dry pair of socks, but after the recent death of a sock I only had 1.5 pairs to work with and decided to use my bed socks. They’re hiking socks anyway, but on TA so far I had been using toe socks. But I figured it was worth a go. Unfortunately, it was becoming apparent that I needed toe socks – the toes on my left foot were rubbing and I could tell I would get blisters. Happily, the remaining sock from the half pair was a left one, so I was able to change that out and keep my right sock as it was. I didn’t think there was anything particularly odd about this, but when the others saw my odd socks at camp later they seemed to think it was an abomination.

My odd socks at camp later – is this really so strange? It was working for me!

They’re selling sections of this land.

Industry observers note that after a bit of effort, I caught Annabel and Sinead again after my sock stop. The bike path went on a bit longer before the trail turned up a side road. We had to walk on the road this time, but it was a quiet road, and quite scenic as it wound its way up the hill. At one point it became a gravel road, and we stopped for a lunch break. After a while on the gravel road, which became progressively narrower and more overgrown, we reached the final 2km to the campsite and the first real track of the day! We knew there was some weather due to be coming in later, and as I walked up (and down) the track, I could hear thunder rumbling in the distance. I was keen to get to camp sooner rather than later, but after the day of gentle climbing on the road, the track felt exceedingly steep and hilly, and my calves were definitely not prepared for such a workout.

Sources indicate that eventually, I popped out of the trees and reached the campsite. Having been here before, I remembered the site as nice but not overly flat and a bit exposed. I was happy to see that there was more flat area than I remembered, although the majority of the site was on quite a hill. The views out across the sea were great. Lindsay was pitching her tent as I arrived, and I pitched mine pretty close, concious of the sloping ground and the other two behind me.

It was funny how the surfaced road stopped so abruptly.

Sven had decided to continue on to Waipu after his short, hitching-heavy day. It was only 3.30pm at this point and if it hadn’t been for the approaching weather and the good company at this campsite, I might have done the same. As I expressed to the others, I’ve been feeling a bit of tension between wanting the physical challenge of pushing for some bigger days, and wanting the trip to last as long as possible so I can enjoy it as much as possible. I think as I move southwards I’ll naturally end up with some bigger days, especially where there are more camping options. Right now, most places are spaced 20-25km apart, and I don’t feel ready for 40-50km days yet! But at the same time, 25km days on easier terrain, like this day, are feeling easy and I get to camp feeling like I haven’t done enough.

In a recent development, as well as the people I had been walking with that day, Bart and Anica were at the campsite. I hadn’t met Anica before, as apparently she has been skipping around a bit. But she seemed cool and we all sat around the table in the shelter, chatting and cooking dinner as we watched the storm roll in. It was a fun place to sit, as we could see bands of rain moving across the ocean towards us. It seemed like the worst of it missed us, but we did get a few heavy showers over the course of the evening. There was a logbook at that campsite, and it provided some good entertainment over the course of the evening. We made prepares to hike out at 7 the next morning, for some reason, and found a trail host in Mangawhai that offered camping for significantly cheaper than the holiday park.

Our tents squashed onto the flattest bit.

One side sun, the other heavy clouds.

This entry made me laugh so much, I had to do a dramatic reading for the others.

#44862. Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (936 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that while they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife.
  • As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts.
  • Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

As expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0.

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

In a recent development, the people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

In a recent development, early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Industry observers note that habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Sources indicate that A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Recent findings suggest that town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

In a recent development, farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

Sources indicate that the incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

Another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

In a recent development, locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

According to recent reports, elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India.

In Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Tech giant.

None of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Manufacturer officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

#44861. Young Climbers Bag Upcoming Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (704 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Young Climbers Bag Upcoming Routes, Including First Ascent, in Rolwaling

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that an energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu.
  • Recent findings suggest that as soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition.
  • Sources indicate that “Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that an energetic foursome of young French climbers had a busy time recently in Nepal’s Rolwaling Valley, east of the Khumbu. Eric Bazon, Pierre Girot, Sophie Jacob, and Kilian Moni did two new routes, including a first ascent of a 5,205m rocky spire and one very difficult line. They then climbed another peak on a “rest” day.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as the climbers reached Rolwaling, they had to change their primary goal, which was in poor condition. Their acclimatization was also progressing more slowly than expected. Instead, they focused their attention on a ridge they saw from their base camp every morning. On October 20, Bazon, Jacob, and Girot set off toward the summit, while Moni waited for them at the base.

Sources indicate that “Before long, the climbing turned vertical, and the ridge became razor-sharp and exposed,” Bazon wrote. The climb took three days on the ridge, bivvies included, and led Bazon, Sophie Jacob, and Pierre Girot to the west summit of ChekiGo (6,128m). It took another full day and one more bivouac to reach base camp.

Cheki Go’s main summit was first climbed in 2005 by Bruce Normand of the UK and Oliver Von Rotz of Switzerland via the west face. A Spanish team led by Mikel Zabalza first reached the west summit via a direct route up the west face in 2017. The team had just returned from bagging the first ascent of Jugal II.

“It was quite an intense experience for a ‘secondary’ project: one that combined rock climbing on mediocre granite, improvised protection, and steep snow ridges, all while hauling our ropes on our backs,” said Bazon.

According to recent reports, the ridge was technical enough to be a good start: 5c on rock and M4 on mixed terrain. In Alpine grades, the team assessed it as TD (very difficult).

The ridge on ChekiGo. Photo: Eric Bazon.

Since the weather forecast looked good for another four days, the team decided to continue climbing. They split into two teams: Bazon and Girot headed for a peak previously climbed by elite American alpinists Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey in 2014: Chukyima Go (6,259m). Like their predecessors, the French team approached the west face from the Naa Valley in Rolwaling.

“There was this direct, narrow, and obvious couloir that simply begged to be climbed,” Bazon reported.

It has been revealed that the climbers at an open bivy. Photo: Eric Bazon.

The next morning, they found the west face in great condition, which allowed them to climb a direct route to the summit along rock cracks, steep ice, and varied mixed terrain.

Industry observers note that it took them two days (October 27-28), with one cold bivy on the face with their feet in their backpacks, to complete the route’s 23 pitches. Their West Face Direct route is 900m long, and the team assessed it as ED (extremely difficult), with M6 on mixed sections, and an Alpine ice grade of AI5.

The photo below shows that the fresh French route, TchikitaMa Go, runs to the right of the previous line opened by the two Americans.

Left: the fresh route opened by the French team, compared, right, to the 2014 line by Domen Kastelic and Sam Hennessey. Photo: Eric Bazon/PlanetMountain.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Sophie Jacob and Kilian Moni went for an unclimbed peak that also rose right in front of their base camp: 5,205m Janjmu. The pair completed the first ascent on an aesthetic 600m line up the north face. They called the route The Eternal Stars (“Les etoiles eternelles”) after some friends who had recently perished.

Sources indicate that “It felt just like being at home in the Alps, with the added challenge of high altitude,” the climbers reported. “We pushed ourselves to the limit, both physically and mentally, across demanding yet incredibly logical pitches.”.

But this was still not enough for the pair. They squeezed in a final climb of Yalung Ri in what they called “a contemplative, active recovery” day. They then finished the trip by paragliding from the summit.

It has been revealed that kilian Moni flies from the top of Yalung Ri. Photo: Kilian Moni.

#44860. Breaking: Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (614 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Duo Completes Baffin Island Circuit By Skiing, Hiking, and Packrafting

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island.
  • According to recent reports, the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital.
  • The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that caleb McDaniels, 25, and Henry Penfold, 22, have completed their impressive expedition around Baffin Island. The Americans combined skiing, hiking, and packrafting to almost circle the world’s fifth-largest island. McDaniels told ExplorersWeb they did about 20% skiing and the rest was evenly split between backpacking and packrafting.

According to recent reports, the pair began and ended in Iqaluit, Nunavut’s capital. The final section of their trip was also the longest, a 1,130km stretch with no villages after Igloolik to resupply. They made light work of it, knocking it out in 40 days and bringing their total distance to 3,262km over 145 days, from their late May start to their return to Iqaluit in mid-October. By then, the oncoming Arctic winter gave them few hours of light to work with.

The pair’s completed route around Baffin Island. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

Industry observers note that with no resupply points, the pair left Igloolik with 82kg of food. They hoped to do it in seven weeks but brought even more food, because they weren’t sure how long that giant giant section would actually take, explained Caleb McDaniels.

“With no way to carry that much weight in our packs, we loaded up our packrafts and paddled the first 400 miles [644km]. Then, for the final 300 miles [483km], we heaved on our packs to walk overland,” they explained.

Industry observers note that the paddling portion went rapidly, aided by some ingenuity. “Much of the time, we were able to sail using our trekking poles as masts and panels cut out of an old tent for sails. Speeding along at over five mph, we did some incredible downwinding, spray flying from our bows.”.

Industry observers note that using makeshift sails. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

Postholing through early winter snow back to Iqaluit. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

Industry observers note that “It was more of a postholing session — we slowly picked our way across snow-covered boulder fields and partly frozen marshlands. Constantly breaking through thin ice over the tundra marshes, we walked in our drysuits to keep our legs and feet dry. Each morning required half an hour of chipping ice and melting out our shoes, which invariably froze solid,” they remarked.

McDaniels and Penfold had planned a roughly circular route around the island, but “we weren’t trying to circumnavigate Baffin,” McDaniels told ExplorersWeb. Two previous parties had circumnavigated the island by dogteam, but McDaniels and Penfold’s route was driven by aesthetic considerations rather than to satisfy a catchy trip definition.

Sources indicate that slogging overland. Photo: Caleb McDaniels.

They chose their route after looking at satellite images and enjoyed both spectacular scenery and some special wildlife sightings, including at least one that was a little too close for comfort.

According to recent reports, “One morning, as I went to fill our water bottles, I stumbled upon a sleeping polar bear hidden behind a low rise. Only a few yards away, it lifted its massive white head and glared at me for a moment before returning to its nap in the sun,” McDaniels wrote. “I carefully retreated behind the rise and yelled over to Henry to get the shotgun and flares out just in case. We quickly packed our boats and got on the water.”.

In Foxe Basin, they almost collided with a sleeping walrus, and on Nettilling Lake, they met one of the resident seals. “He was immensely curious and not at all afraid. He swam around our boats for half an hour, playing with our stern lines and swimming back and forth between us. At one point, I put my hand into the water, and he brushed it with his nose!”.

Americans Bag Major First Ascent in Pakistan

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m).
  • Industry observers note that this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5.
  • Industry observers note that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans Dane Steadman and Cody Winckler, awarded with a Piolet d’Or in 2025 after the first ascent of Yashkuk Sar, have done a similar monster 1,800m-long new route on the north face of Sosbun Brakk (6,414m). This time, Grant Stewart joined them for this off-season climb in the Karakoram.

Industry observers note that this first ascent of the peak’s north face included difficulties up to M7, WI5. The climbers had to overcome several obstacles before even setting foot on the face. Like many other alpine-style teams this season, they were originally planning to climb another peak. But instead of adapting because of washed-out trails, they had bureaucratic concerns. Their permit, obtained 10 months earlier, was revoked some weeks before their departure. They had to promptly find a different goal.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the airline misplaced Winckler’s baggage — every adventurer’s nightmare. Somehow, the outfitter sent it to base camp some days later. Then, Steadman had to overcome serious Acute Mountain Sickness in base camp. Their acclimatization was hampered by freak spells of bad weather. Finally, the line on Sosbun Brakk they initially chose was too hard and risky because of a hanging serac they only spotted after they began.

The team’s lonely base camp. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“Back at BC, it was time to rest, regroup, and contemplate a totally different line that we’d seen from on the wall, which gave us new hope,” Steadman recalled.

Off to the north face. Photo: Dane Steadman.

According to recent reports, on October 1, the three climbers set off on that potential newly introduced line. “Instead of angling left up hard mixed ground above the cone as before, we made an arcing traverse right, across an ice apron, to gain runnels on the right side of the face,” Steadman explained.

The team gained 800m on that first day and set their first bivouac on a snowy arete, just in time to be slammed by a violent storm that kept them in their tent the whole next day.

In a recent development, steep mixed terrain. Photo: Dane Steadman.

A tarp to protect the team’s bivouac from falling spindrift. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“In the morning, we made a gamble for the top by leaving the tent and starting up a massive gully system,” Steward wrote. “At its top, we reached another dead end in a huge serac barrier. To escape this, Dane committed to a visionary pitch, casting off up a blank slab to eventually reach an ice smear.”.

Chaotic, difficult rocky sections. Photo: Dane Steadman.

“A huge serac to our right and smooth slabs out left posed a serious question; eight meters of sideways teetering on tiny gneissic edges and a miraculous rock thread were the answer,” said Steadman.

Industry observers note that “We continued up the massive hanging glacier to reach the hallucinatory final headwall of steep ice/mixed climbing and mushroom-weaving lunacy,” Stewart continued. “One final traverse with 1,800m of exposure under our feet and a magically appearing, dead-vertical ice tongue led us to the summit ridge.”.

A totally vertical section. Photo: Grant Stewart.

According to recent reports, “The wild terrain on the upper mountain took longer than we wanted,” Steadman admitted. By the time they finally reached the summit, it was 4 pm, the storm was coming the following day, and they still had a long way (and many rappels) down.

Summit picture on Sosbun Brakk. Left to right, Dane Steadman, Grant Stewart, and Cody Wrincker. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that “The sun would set around 6 pm, so we threaded the first of 35 rappels and started down. Long after dark, we finally arrived back at our bivy ledge at around 5,800m,” Steadman recalled.

The storm was not supposed to start until noon the following day, but it was already snowing at 8 am, with still 1,200 vertical meters of descent to go.

Sources indicate that rappelling down the route. Photo: Dane Steadman.

In a recent development, “Before long, we were caught in a proper storm,” Stewart explained. “We committed to a faster and hopefully safer descent by rappelling down the west rib to the Sokha/Sosbun col. By the time we reached the col, we could barely communicate over the screaming southwest wind.”.

After some scary rappels in high winds down the serac band, the climbers finally reached a sheltered section of the face. They still had to deal with heavy spindrift coming from above until finally, at around 4 pm, they touched down on the glacier. And yet, the adventure was not over — especially for Grant Stewart:.

It has been revealed that following Dane, I took maybe 10 steps when I felt the ground under me crack. Instinctively, I jumped and landed on my stomach as a huge crevasse swallowed the ground behind me. Soaking wet, we began postholing into the wan light of a mesmerizing white out.

[We stuck] to the center of the glacier as avalanches rumbled down all around in the whirling snow. After a strange eternity, the ragged colors of a tent appeared and we were greeted by ecstatic dancing, significant hugs, and endless cups of chai from (our BC crew) Ibrahim and Idrees.

Industry observers note that happy climbers and base camp crew after a safe return from the summit. Photo: Dane Steadman.

Recent findings suggest that the team didn’t report their success and the details of the climb until they returned home. And then, the first words of appraisal were not for the route itself, but for the mountains and people of Gilgit-Baltistan.

“It’s a unique place…where continents and cultures collide. Trips there, while often difficult, are rewarding in ways hard to describe simply,” Steadman stated. This was his third trip to the Karakoram, a place he has fallen in love with.

Weekend Warm-Up: Assynt

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (391 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.
  • Industry observers note that the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries.
  • But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Assynt, subtitled “Home is where the croft is,” is a short documentary that brings viewers to the Scottish Highland community of Assynt, where residents live on traditional crofts.

Industry observers note that the croft is a uniquely Scottish term, describing the smaller, less fertile plots of land that poorer people were forced onto, following the infamous Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries. Crofters lived on their crofts and farmed for subsistence, grazing sheep on shared land. Unable to support themselves on the croft alone, most also worked in fishing, kelp, or peat to support themselves.

It was a very hard life. But Lewis MacAskill, whom the viewer is soon introduced to, doesn’t see it that way. He is one of just over a thousand residents of Assynt, who chose to stay and continue the crofting tradition.

“I regard the croft as an extension of who I am as a person,” MacAskill explains.

The small community of Assynt. Photo: Screenshot.

In a recent development, macAskill introduces us to some of the other members of the community. Anna is a sheepdog owner and trainer, whom we see herding sheep using the same techniques people here have used for centuries. Stuart is a passionate fisherman, who shares his love of Assynt’s natural landscape with his young son.

Sources indicate that we also meet some of the creatives who have, MacAskill states, been drawn by the unique landscape and material culture. We see a potter using local materials, a fiddler, and a spinner on her spinning wheel.

Sources indicate that the spinning wheel came to Europe from the Middle East by the 13th century, and was widely adopted by the 18th century, replacing the older drop spindle and distaff. Photo: Screenshot.

Recent findings suggest that macAskill moved to the croft a decade ago, and doesn’t regret it. Having grown up visiting every summer, he has always felt drawn to the land and knows others feel the same. But a small, isolated community like Assynt is constantly in danger of depopulation. MacAskill hopes that people keep choosing to move back and stay, heeding the same call he did.

The film ends on this note, with a montage of scenes from life in Assynt and the landscape it sits in, while an elderly crofter sings a traditional Scottish song of homecoming.

#44856. Tech Report: 🌙🥾Beyond the Last Road: Into the Wild Sierras ⛰️✨

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1532 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 🌙🥾Beyond the Last Road: Into the Wild Sierras ⛰️✨

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I woke up at 3 a.m.
  • I turned north onto the trail as the morning sun began to kiss the high desert sky.
  • According to recent reports, my backpack was heavy with a fresh resupply, and now a bear can added to the load.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I woke up at 3 a.m. to a clear night with bright stars. Eager to be on the trail, I used an electric kettle to boil water for oatmeal and coffee. With my bag packed and chores complete, I started walking down the road at 5 a.m., alone in the dark.

I turned north onto the trail as the morning sun began to kiss the high desert sky.

According to recent reports, my backpack was heavy with a fresh resupply, and now a bear can added to the load. The meadow was beautiful. The trail was sandy, causing the hike to be slow. I could feel the temperature dropping as the trail approached the South Fork Kern River. The sound of water was getting louder.

Industry observers note that passing through the campground where I had camped for three nights, I realized this was the last road crossing on trail for the next 250 miles. The thought was both intimidating and exhilarating. I signed the official PCTA logbook before heading north, alone into the incredible Sierra Nevada Mountains.

The trail twisted through large white boulders before reaching a wood bridge crossing the Kern River.

Two miles later, I crossed my first of many Sierra streams on a log.

Sources indicate that the trail opened up to a beautiful valley on my left. I stopped to enjoy the view of Beck Meadow, with a cabin off in the distance across the grassy meadow. I half expected to see a bear walking to the stream. Shedding some layers, I suddenly found myself dodging a bird flying at me. Swiftly tucking my hat and coat into my backpack, I continued my ridgeline hike.

After hiking another three miles uphill, I was exhausted. I chose to clear my own slightly slanted spot away from the water rather than use the established spot right next to Cow Creek. I wanted to avoid the cold and condensation in the morning.

Recent findings suggest that it was cold, so I bundled up and packed my gear in the dark. At 6 a.m., I continued my hike up Cow Creek.

In a recent development, the morning sun began to lighten the sky. The creek came alive with little waterfalls tumbling over the rocks. Bright red snowflowers emerged from the dirt, adding splashes of color to the landscape.

As I passed the Monache Meadow Trail junction, the trees opened up enough to give me glimpses of the PCT winding through the mountains to the south.

In a recent development, I stopped to enjoy the view and take a break. While resting, Ellery, Jug, and Shrimp Gut caught up with me. After introducing ourselves, I asked if they had seen a marmot yet. Excitedly, I told them we would probably start seeing marmots soon. They were just as excited about the possibility of seeing marmots as I was.

According to recent reports, as I climbed above 10,000 feet, the trail became sandy and rocky. I passed around snow-covered Olancha Peak, a memorable ending to my attempted hike in 2018. I also spotted my first marmot!

I hiked among white sage, lupine, manzanita, and towering conifer trees.

Recent findings suggest that taking a long break at Death Canyon Creek, I met Vienna and Cordon Blu. Tired, I attempted to nap as unseen jets boomed overhead, passing behind the white, fluffy clouds.

Industry observers note that hiking past beautiful stone spires, I walked along the ridge, enjoying views of the desert below. Exhausted but motivated, I wanted to hike more miles. I stopped briefly to watch my first glider plane.

The boulders looked as if a giant had stacked them on top of each other.

Seven miles after enjoying the ridge views, I stopped for the night at beautiful Diaz Creek.

I needed to reach the Lone Pine Post Office before it closed on Friday because it wasn’t open on weekends.

With my alarm going off at 4 a.m., I struggled to get going in the damp cold. After coffee and oatmeal, I laid my quilt out to dry in the sun.

Listening to music through my headphones, I was startled by a hiker named Agnes. She had just seen a bear by her tent and pointed him out to me as he ran off down the creek.

Hiking up a hill, I noticed a strange smell. About 30 seconds later, I met a couple with smaller backpacks and a dog hiking in the opposite direction. The strange smell was perfume. After petting the dog, I continued down the hill and almost missed the trail to Horseshoe Meadows. Stopping at a creek just before the parking lot, I took a break and got myself organized for hitching.I watched two more people and a dog hike down another trail toward the parking lot. I should have asked them for a ride, I thought, as I washed my face in the cold water.

Reaching the Cottonwood Pass parking lot, I saw a guy in a Sprinter van offering trail magic in the form of soda and Wi-Fi.

Grabbing a soda, I talked with a foreign couple hiking the PCT before walking off in search of a ride.

Recent findings suggest that hiking across the parking lot, I saw a small truck backing out of a parking spot. I started waving my arms as they put the truck in gear. Thankfully, they saw me and waited.

Sources indicate that when I reached the truck, I realized it was the two hikers from the creek, Tyler and James. I threw my pack in the back of the truck and squeezed into the little back seat with their older, medium-sized dog.

As we were about to start our descent out of the mountains, we saw a hang glider standing on the edge of a cliff.

Recent findings suggest that we stopped to watch. She patiently waited about 10 minutes for the wind to be right. With a storm approaching, she needed to get off the cliff. A few minutes later, the wind was just right, and she jumped, soaring into the desert valley.

I asked to be dropped off at the post office, expecting three packages: my food, the stickers I’d been out of since the day after Tehachapi, and a thicker merino wool base layer.

I left the post office with only my food. The base layer was now expected Monday, and the stickers had been shipped UPS, so they were sent back.

Walking to the grocery store, I bought a half quart of ice cream and a 20 oz. soda. With my arms full, I walked to a nearby restaurant and sat down at an outside table.

I drank the soda and ate half the ice cream before walking across the street to Elevation Sierra Adventure Essentials.

According to recent reports, elevation has a fenced-in outdoor area that doubles as a hiker hangout. There, I saw Marble, Pickles, and Electrolyte, along with a hiker named Too Clean and a few others.

As the afternoon went on, the weather looked like it might rain.

It has been revealed that hungry for Chinese, we made our way to the Merry Go Round. Along the way, we ran into Fairy and invited her to join us.

The meal was hot and delicious, with plenty left over for later.

“Establish harmony and balance in your life.”.

A Leaky Tent Is a Piece of Paradise: 20 Young Writers on Finding a Place in the Natural World was suggested as a book to read by Tyler and James.

#44855. Te Araroa day 21: Is this what it feels like to be famous?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1906 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Te Araroa day 21: Is this what it feels like to be famous?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18km, Waorahi Campsite to trail host in Mangawhai Village.
  • For some reason, we had decided that we needed to leave camp at 7 this morning, despite only having 18km to go.
  • Industry observers note that me, Annabel and Sinéad in the morning sun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

18km, Waorahi Campsite to trail host in Mangawhai Village.

For some reason, we had decided that we needed to leave camp at 7 this morning, despite only having 18km to go. The weather was good when we left, but everything was very damp from rain and dew. The morning started with a slightly overgrown grassy section, so inevitably we all ended up soaked in the first 5 minutes. Still, the light coming through the trees was very pretty and we soon got out onto some gravel road/track. This went quite steeply down until we met the road at around 8am. After crossing the road, we ended up on some farmland. We watched a farmer skillfully herding sheep with a Gator, and were able to look back and see the forest where we camped the previous night.

Industry observers note that me, Annabel and Sinéad in the morning sun. Photo by Lindsay.

This is the photo I had stopped to take!

The gang ready to start the farmland section of the day.

A view back to the mountains where we slept the night before, feat Anica.

Sources indicate that the track went up and down some hills, and after a short while we hit the Mangawhai cliff walkway. I have done this walk before, when I was WWOOFing in the area. At the time, I think I was a bit burnt out to wonderful coastal views, so I didn’t really appreciate it fully. But now, walking with people who hadn’t been there before, I was able to more fully appreciate that it was actually very pretty. Eventually the track took us down to the black sand beach, where I got my feet wet again with a poorly-judged jump over a stream. The tide was quite far in, so we had to hop over a few rocks and skirt around some pools before making it to the surf club. Sinéad, ever the water baby, wanted to swim and I reassured her that we would shortly be hitting the beach again on the other side of the headland. By the time we got there, though, it was starting to spit rain, and we sat under a tree to shelter while Sinead and Annabel took a dip. It was a shame the weather didn’t hold out, as I had been keen to join them before it started raining.

Industry observers note that the others found this funny because it sounds like walkers are the hazard. I was too preoccupied with the terrible graphic design to notice; centre aligned and left aligned, with the hazards weirdly far to the right. What is going on here?!

Me on the coast track. Photo by Sinéad.

Walking along the beach at the end of the coast path.

The others pick their way over the rocks.

Recent findings suggest that after a very short walk further up the beach, we came to a gelato van that I had thought was only there in the afternoons (it was only 11am). Was it too early for an ice cream? Of course not! We had a good chat with the guy there – he and his wife make all their own ice cream from whatever ingredients they can get their hands on, and there were some really interesting flavours. I had a tangelo sorbet, which was amazing. We had previously been talking about stopping for coffee in Mangawhai Heads, but after my ice cream and the multiple breaks, I really wanted to keep moving and cover some ground. Anica came with me, and the others found a cafe. There were only 7km to go to where we would be staying that night, and we weren’t supposed to arrive before 4pm, so there was really no rush. But I needed to resupply on the way, and I wanted to do laundry in the town, as for some reason I hadn’t bothered doing it on my day off.

The official route out of town was a road walk, but I saw a promising-looking sign for an off-road track that looked to be heading in the right direction. I decided to risk it for a biscuit, and it worked out well and cut out some boring road. After a bit, I arrived at the new shopping centre where the New World supermarket was located. Finding myself on the wrong side of the road, I looked for somewhere to cross. But I didn’t see anywhere, and between the road and the pavement was a drainage ditch planted with oioi. It really irks me when places are so clearly not built with pedestrians in mind, and unfortunately that’s quite common in NZ. I ended up pushing through the oioi, stepping over the ditch and crossing the road to repeat on the other side. Then I was finally at New World.

It has been revealed that I realised that although I knew how many days I wanted to resupply for, I wasn’t really sure how much food I already had. I decided to sit on the ground outside the supermarket and get all my food out so I could have a look. Anica appeared and started to do the same. As hikers, we were already conspicuous for our large backpacks, stinky clothes, and the fact that we were walking rather than driving to the supermarket. Sitting on the floor with food everywhere was definitely not a normal thing to do, but luckily no one seemed to mind. They did notice though. In the 10-15 minutes we were sat there sorting and eating, several people wished us luck or asked how things were going. A little girl asked ‘Mummy, are those trampers?’ to which the mum replied that we were. It’s a good thing I’m not too self-concious about being percieved in public – thru-hiking would be a nightmare if you didn’t like being noticed!

Looking down at Mangawhai Heads.

Industry observers note that in the supermarket, I nearly spiralled when I couldn’t find dried peas or lentils. Luckily, they were just in a different aisle to usual. I probably got way too much fresh and heavy food (cucumber, cherry tomatoes, pepper, kale, hummus, mayo) but who cares. I will carry a significant weight penalty to have good lunches! Otherwise, my resupply didn’t seem too large. I haven’t really nailed the quantities yet, and I always seem to have quite a bit left over from the previous stretch.

In a recent development, the next item on the agenda was laundry, which I was cursing myself for not doing on my day off. It was a couple more kilometres down the road to Mangawhai Village, where we were staying and where the laundrette was. The official TA path takes a nice boardwalk through some mangroves, but I had to leave it to go to the supermarket and I couldn’t be bothered to backtrack to rejoin it, so I walked down the main road. After a cloudy start to the day, the sun had come out and it was getting pretty warm. My pack felt reasonably heavy but I felt fine with the weight; I kind of enjoyed the feeling of a pack full of food.

Sources indicate that I reached the village and scoped out the laundry situation. It sold detergent, which was excellent news as I didn’t really have a plan B for that. What was less excellent was that the machines needed some kind of special card, which cost $3 to buy and could only be charged in increments of $5 (and naturally, the cost of laundry was not in increments of $5). I didn’t have much choice though, so I went to the nearby toilet to change into my rain gear. Despite recently repacking my bag while I was sorting my resupply, it had not occured to me to locate my laundry, or put it at the top of my bag. So now I had to empty my bag, again, onto the street outside the toilet. I bought the card, topped it up, bought the soap, and a good $15 poorer I was finally able to start my laundry.

It must be a special torture of thru-hiking, to sweat your ass off sitting in an overheated laundrette wearing your plastic-y rain gear with nothing on underneath. I could feel the drops of sweat sliding down my back as I watched my laundry spinning. The one good thing about this place was that there were charging sockets, which I made full use of. Partway through my laundry cycle, a guy came in and asked me for probably the eighth time that day if I was doing the long walk. He seemed really nice though and since there wasn’t much else to do, I chatted with him a bit. I let him pick my pack up to see how much it weighed and he looked impressed. I did point out I had just done a resupply! He asked if I had a place to stay and if I needed anything, and I remarked honestly that I didn’t need anything now, but if he had been 10 minutes earlier I would have asked to use his laundry card! He then offered his number in case I did think of something, but I declined. I really did have everything under control and taking random guys’ numbers is not something I’m in the habit of doing.

After what felt like an eternity, the wash cycle finished. I couldn’t bear the feeling of my sweaty rain jacket anymore so I put my damp bra on and the rest of my laundry in the drier, which was in expensive increments of 10 minutes. I was surprised but pleased when everything was virtually dry after the first 10 minutes. I was still early for the place we were staying, as we weren’t supposed to show up before 4. I considered texting the others to find out where they were, but decided I ought to act like the independent person I normally am and found a small park to sit in and wait.

At 4pm, I showed up. The first thing I noticed that the place was super cute – an orchard with a little cabin, a toilet, and plenty of space between the trees for tents. The second thing I noticed was someone I hadn’t seen in a while – along with the others I was expecting, Zoe was there! For anyone who doesn’t remember, Zoe started the beach on the same day as me and we passed 100km together, but I hadn’t seen her since Waitangi. It was great to catch up, have a (cold) shower, dry out the rest of my stuff, and relax. At around 6pm a few of us went to the takeaway to get chips, and we enjoyed chips with a variety of supermarket extras. Greens were prominent on the menu!

#44854. Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

Florida Man Finishes Four Corners Walk Across America

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (369 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk.
  • Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida.
  • Recent findings suggest that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

Kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Recent findings suggest that over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His plans expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

Recent findings suggest that on October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Recent findings suggest that edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

It has been revealed that A cross-country walking journey, Edwards says, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

According to recent reports, the end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.
