#44853. High Sierra Storm — John Muir Trail Day 20

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3207 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

High Sierra Storm — John Muir Trail Day 20

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the rain fell off-and-on throughout the night.
  • Sources indicate that lying warm in my cozy bed in Red’s Meadow, I tried to discern whether I was dreaming (asleep) or daydreaming (awake).
  • When I saw that it was 6:30, I thought, “Well, breakfast starts at 7 a.m., so I had better get going.”   I got dressed, got ready, and got mostly packed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  43,704 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  25:17.

According to recent reports, the rain fell off-and-on throughout the night. It was a light rain, as I discovered when I left my cabin to pee. It felt like the threat of a serious storm may have been overblown, to coin a pun.

Sources indicate that lying warm in my cozy bed in Red’s Meadow, I tried to discern whether I was dreaming (asleep) or daydreaming (awake). I was thinking about the pleasures of life and the inevitability of death. Lighthearted stuff like that. Maybe I was dreaming and asleep, and death is really not inevitable after all? The advice I found on the cabin wall was a bit more down-to-earth!

Red’s Meadow Rules might apply anywhere, right?

When I saw that it was 6:30, I thought, “Well, breakfast starts at 7 a.m., so I had better get going.”   I got dressed, got ready, and got mostly packed. I assembled the remainder of my resupply, what I was not going to take with me. This was mostly a lot of M&M weight and one excess freeze-dried packet. Then I headed off to the restaurant, where I was first in line for breakfast.

Being first in the morning? That was new for me! I got a couple of eggs, bacon, a couple of pancakes (of which I ate only one), coffee, and orange juice. It all seemed very civilized as I chatted with the people at the table next to me. They were from my home state, from Seattle. She was a baker and he was a high-rise window cleaner.

It has been revealed that after a stop at the privy, and a stop to return my key, I got back to my room. At 8:00, I prepared to depart. I recognized that my hiking gloves were in bad shape, but a pair I found abandoned in the laundry were three sizes too small. So I stuck with what I had.

Sources indicate that the gloves would not last beyond the trip, but were still usable. You can see I faithfully splinted my mallet finger.

According to recent reports, just about then the rain picked up. So, in my cozy little room, I put on my dry rain poncho.

In a recent development, putting on a poncho is easy with a friend to help. Alone, it can be more challenging. The main problem is that you cannot see your own back. You presume that you’re covering everything properly, but since you can’t see it, you can’t be certain. But I thought I got it.

I headed down the stairs outside my cabin and out into the rain.

In a recent development, this was a popular hiking area where a lot of different trails intermingle and crisscross. It was therefore potentially easy to get a little lost. I saw a workable route on my app that went past the Devil’s Postpile, so I took that one. Why not check it out?

As I approached it, the first people I met remarked, “Oh, the Devil’s Postpile entails a long hike up to a high point.”.

I thought, “I don’t really have time to do that.”.

Then the next group I met said, “Oh, it’s a short little hop just up to the top of that hill there and down.”.

Sources indicate that once again, I marveled at how different the perceptions of different people can be, when describing the same thing. I figured, “When am I ever going to be here again? I may as well go see the Devil’s Postpile.”  So, I started off. It was an uphill climb, but it was short. The second description was more accurate.

Devil’s Postpile, showing the columns.

In a recent development, where the mostly-hexagonal basalt columns stuck out from the hillside was most dramatic. On the top they formed a sort of tiled floor, like finely paved flagstones of basalt that fit together perfectly. I took some pictures, then I came down.

Devil’s Postpile, showing a wet paved floor.

Overall, it was less than overwhelming, but still interesting. As I proceeded on my way, I came to a trail crossing. To test the direction, I went straight ahead for about 100 yards and then checked my FarOut app. It indicated that I was going the wrong way. So, I went back to the crossing and took the other trail.

Subsequently, I looked at the map of the area and realized I would have traveled a shorter distance by going in my original direction. The app added about a half mile to my day. Not a substantial deal, but why?

Recent findings suggest that at that point getting to my destination, Garnet Lake, represented an elevation gain of over 3,500 feet, and an elevation loss of 1,500 feet. It looked like a lot of up and down, and overall, a really, hard day. But I was feeling strong, and I was passing a lot of younger people on the trail.

The route was very good, not super steep, so that the elevation gains were manageable. I hiked them without stopping and catching my breath every 60 steps. Surprised at how fast I was moving, and how much progress I was making, I started to think, “Well, my goal is Garnet Lake. That’s my planned schedule. But maybe I can go the extra two-and-a-half miles up to Thousand Island Lake? This will put me ahead of schedule in the days ahead.”.

Stream and Meadow en Route to Garnet Lake (Storm Threatening).

According to recent reports, as I was thinking all these thoughts about the future, about the huge miles I was going to pound out, the weather let up. I was not so foolish as to take off the rain poncho yet, but I doffed the hood so I could see better and feel the breeze and hear better.

Up to this point I had been leapfrogging a group of four guys. This time, now that I could hear, I asked the lead fellow what their story was. He told me, in a British accent, “We are here section hiking, doing a LASH (Long Ass Section Hike) on the John Muir Trail, finally finishing it in fact. We are doing it with our dad; it is just our dad and his three sons.”.

Recent findings suggest that I was moved by that, particularly as someone alienated from his own two sisters, to see their family unity. It warmed my heart, actually, and before hiking on I told them so.

I had set one p.m. as the target time to have my lunch. Yet around 12:15, the clouds thinned so that the sun was strong enough to cast somewhat of a shadow through them. Just then, during that period of slight sunshine, I had a chance to have my lunch on a rock overlooking a lovely lake. But no, I remained determined I was going to wait until one o’clock.

The rain had (temporarily) stopped when I passed this lake.

According to recent reports, the trail turned sharply downhill to another lake, and I realized that most of my 1,500-foot elevation loss on the day would be descents down to lakes. This time, when I got down to  the lakeshore, it was finally lunchtime, and I stopped to eat near the shore. Now there was no longer any sign of the sun, and the clouds were massing, but I parked my gear, took out my food, and sat on a rock overlooking the lake.

My lunch site (before the weather turned).

Recent findings suggest that I had selected a tamale for lunch, a favorite high-calorie treat. As I ate my tamale, it got a little chillier, a little windier, and I started to feel the first few drops of rain. I finished up the tamale, ate a Snickers bar, ate some jerky, and by then a little more rain was falling. So I cut short the lunch, finished up what I had taken out, and quickly packed it up. Before returning to the trail, I put my rain gear back on, no longer hopeful that I was done needing it for the day.

According to recent reports, at that point I still felt strong, and I was still thinking I might make it to Thousand Island Lake. If not, well, my original destination at Garnet Lake would be fine too.

On the trail in my poncho, long before it got really bad….

Recent findings suggest that as I continued hiking, the rain fell harder and heavier, and the wind increased steadily. Visibility dropped and the rain turned into a true downpour. While I was dry enough under the poncho, my arms and hands, holding my poles, were sopping wet. The same was true of my legs and feet. They were all getting cold. There was so much water on the trail I could no longer avoid walking through mud puddles – the whole trail was a mud puddle!

A the wind increased, the rain was not falling straight down, but falling at a wind-blown angle. Also, because the mountains shape the wind, it came from different angles at different moments. As I gained elevation, it also became gustier, buffeting me in my rain poncho that served almost like a large wet sail.

Recent findings suggest that as the wind blew harder, I could hear it even with my hood on, as a roaring sound. Sometimes it would abate for a few minutes, only to resume with increased force. At one point, I heard an especially loud blast howling toward me and just had time to turn my back to brace myself when it hit. I am sure that gust was at least 50 MPH and possibly more. The rain was relentless too. This was a true High Sierra storm!

Recent findings suggest that shortly after that, three people passed by me. They dropped a quick “Hello” as they went by, nice enough, but they were clearly focused on the trail. I saw that they had ropes, and ice axes; clearly, they were climbers. I wondered what an ice axe is for in the summer when there’s no ice? As they were not moving that much faster than I was, I resolved to speed up a little to keep pace with them. Actually, I was a little worried about my safety, and I thought it might be good to remain in shouting distance, just in case….

I kept up for about a mile, all of us fighting the wind and rain, but then they turned left at a fork in the trail and I continued right towards Garnet Lake. I was alone again.

I passed another couple of people, going down, and I asked, “Are we crazy, are we literally insane to be out here?”  Through the steady downpour, they looked at me like I really was crazy.

In a recent development, taking pictures of green rocks in the middle of a rainstorm? Maybe I really am insane!

At one point, I passed a tent pitched by the side of the path. It looked so cozy and nice, I felt a pang of jealousy. But I kept going.

Industry observers note that the problem is, you don’t know when it’s going to end, right? I mean, it could clear up in an hour. Or maybe two hours? Or maybe five hours? Or maybe 12 hours? In each of those cases, if you knew, really knew, then the decision “What should I do?” would be so much clearer. If “one hour” then you should keep going,  it will be over soon. If “12 hours” then you should find the next reasonably good camp site and hunker down until the morning.

It has been revealed that the next guy coming down helped me to decide. He said, “You know, the weather conditions are even worse higher up, and it’s more exposed.”  That meant at my presumed destination, Garnet Lake, the weather would be worse, finding a camp site would be harder, and, in the wind, pitching my tent would be a nightmare.

Sources indicate that A little further on, then, I pulled aside, off the trail. I spotted a father and his son there, also pulled over, just about 10 yards away from me. I started talking with them.

The son was in his early teens, and it was his first hiking trip! So, I explained to him the concept of Type Two fun and assured him he was getting GREAT stories to tell his pals when he got back to school. They were very much thinking about turning around, and going back down. I understood; it was miserable! They’d started from a meadow below, and were now thinking of just going back to that meadow, where there was even a chance of getting a shuttle to town. They decided to turn back.

In a recent development, before leaving, however, the father pointed out that a little deeper in the shelter of the woods there was a potential tent site. I went and looked at it. It seemed drained. I mean, obviously it was soaking wet, but it didn’t have a puddle in it. I thought, “Okay, forget Garnet Lake, I’m going to try this.”.

Industry observers note that here’s the problem with rain. Hiking in the rain isn’t actually so bad, if you have rain gear and stay warm by moving steadily. But making camp or breaking camp in the rain is a misery. So it was in this case.

According to recent reports, I was trying to stay as dry as possible, trying to create a little dry haven under the trees. But the rain was still pouring down. I did my best, but the dry haven became a wet mess in a very short time. As fast as I could go was nowhere near fast enough. The ground sheet, which I staked immediately, so it wouldn’t go flying in the wind, was soaking wet well before I put the tent down over it. Then the tent was sopping wet by the time I got the rain fly over it. That created my dry space, but it wasn’t a dry space anymore, because it had been rained on heavily for, I don’t know, five minutes? Eight minutes? Maybe even 10 minutes?

However long it took to pitch the tent, my next move was to shove my whole soaking wet backpack in there. Very few items, like my completely soaking rain gear and my hiking poles, did not go in. The last soggy item to go inside the tent was… me.

According to recent reports, once inside, I was dismayed to see there were major puddles of water all over the floor of the tent. I was really worried; I wondered if I had torn or compromised my tent floor and water was leaking in that way. I came inside with my shoes on initially, urgently escaping the rain. But this was stupid, because I hadn’t set down my sleeping pad to cushion the floor. In a site like this, that I had not scoured for rocks and twigs beforehand, there was a real danger of tearing the tent floor.

What to do? I took my bandana and soaked it up on the tent floor, then reached outside the tent flap and squeezed it out like a sponge. I did this again and again and again. Eventually I saw that the amount of water on the tent floor was decreasing, and more water did not seem to be coming in. That was a relief! I continued until the floor was only wet, and no longer soaking.

Then I lay there for a while, just resting and listening to the storm still gushing water and roaring wind outside. But I realized, there was a certain danger of hypothermia if I continued in my state of paralysis. I roused myself then and got my shoes off and into the covered vestibule; I got my soaking wet socks out there too.

Recent findings suggest that the great news was that between my rain poncho, and the plastic bag liner inside my pack, the pack contents were all dry. I took off my shirt and my shorts, and I put on a dry shirt from inside my pack, and dry pants, and fresh socks. Now I was feeling better.

Sources indicate that I did not worry about bears. If they wanted to eat me or my food in this weather, they were welcome to us. In the tent I opened my bear cannister and selected a packet of freeze-dried dinner for cold soaking. It was a chicken alfredo, or something like that, a chicken in a white sauce with noodles. It ranked among the blandest meals I ever ate, but it was calories. I forced myself to eat every bite of it.

Recent findings suggest that I stretched out my pad and pulled my dry sleeping bag out of its stuff sack. To stay warm, I put my puffy on, my shirt on, my pants on, and my wool socks on. After about an hour or two, the heaviest rain did start to abate, though it didn’t end. To the sound of the wind searching and seeking and moving through the mountaintops, I dozed off.

When I woke again at 9 p.m., the downpour had been over for a couple of hours, the wind was down, but it was still occasionally dripping rain. The temperature had dropped, but wearing dry clothes I was warm enough.

It has been revealed that I realized that instead of the vision of hiking beyond my intended destination, I was now a couple of miles short of where I intended to camp. If the rain resumed in the morning, I was not going to leave my tent. However, if it was dry, I would face a long day.

As I dozed off again, I listened to the sound of raindrops falling on my tent from the pine needles overhead. To my surprise, I found it soothing and I slept.

Adventure Links of the Week

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web.
  • Sources indicate that yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock.
  • Recent findings suggest that A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Sources indicate that yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

Recent findings suggest that A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

Sources indicate that the Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Industry observers note that jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

It has been revealed that A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Sources indicate that matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

He Felt Stuck in Newly introduced York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

This Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Recent findings suggest that men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

According to recent reports, A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Industry observers note that two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

Food, so much food! (Day 166)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (668 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s resupply day today!
  • Industry observers note that we can never pass up a private pond beach though.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve talked about us rationing food and being hungry more often lately, but today I hit a fresh low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Follow Gerjan "Hungry" Hertgers.

In a recent development, it’s resupply day today! We have 10 miles to go to Jo Mary road where Shaw’s will deliver our food drop. We have to be there before 2 pm, so let’s get going!

Industry observers note that we can never pass up a private pond beach though. Even though the view is simply amazing, our attention went to an exploring ladybug. Climbing on top of a fire ring and us creating stick bridges to help her find the grass again. What more do you need for entertainment?

Recent findings suggest that I’ve talked about us rationing food and being hungry more often lately, but today I hit a fresh low. Just before the road crossing I got hit with a crazy dizzy spell and I had to sit down for a second. So this is what Dreamcatcher is usually experiencing, huh.

I’m hallucinating too. I swear I can smell a grill in the distance. My mind is playing tricks on me. Luckily, we hit the road and got our resupply! We can’t start eating like crazy though, since this resupply is just as tight as the last one. But luckily for us, my dad is here too! With sandwiches!! Score! I basically inhaled it before I could say any words. It’s good to see my dad again! But he didn’t look ready to hike. His knee is still bothering him too much. He made the hard decision to definitively get off trail and give up on reaching Katahdin. That’s a hard pill to swallow, for us both to be honest. But it’s the right decision. It’s just not worth it to cause your body irreparable harm for ego. I’m super proud of him. For getting this far, but also for making the hard but smart decision. He got a ride back to Shaw’s and will go to Millinocket soon. We’ll see him there in a couple of days.

Sources indicate that in the meantime we saw a sign: “Hot grill cold drinks across the bridge – Chilly P”. My nose wasn’t fooling me! There’s actually a trail angel in the middle of the 100-mile having a grill going!

According to recent reports, chilly P is awesome. He truly is super chill and grilled us an insane amount of burgers. I had four, on top of the sandwich I already ate. I would be lying if I said I couldn’t eat more. There’s cold drinks, beers, fruit, snacks; basically everything a group of underfed hikers could ever need. It’s simply the best. We spent a good amount of time here, chilling with Chilly P.

It has been revealed that after continuing, we came across a day hiker giving us some snacks. I guess our trail magic meter must have been full again! We’re so grateful.

According to recent reports, at the end of the day, we reached a beautiful tent site on a peninsula on another lake, with mesmerizing skies. What a day.

#44849. Latest Update: Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • Recent findings suggest that hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • Brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their looks to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Recent findings suggest that hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

Brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

It has been revealed that indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

It has been revealed that satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

Another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She plans to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also plan to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

Sources indicate that at least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

In a recent development, satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 proposal is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

Sources indicate that A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

Industry observers note that gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni claims his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and proposal to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

According to recent reports, the Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a newly introduced route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team intends a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

Sources indicate that the wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and proposal to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

#44848. Industry News: A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (647 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Industry observers note that everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Industry observers note that everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” stated Baia.

According to recent reports, he claims the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In a recent development, in addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

Industry observers note that after their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health challenges. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick fresh layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

Recent findings suggest that “Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

Sources indicate that “Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

Industry observers note that that answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

In a recent development, in fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

Sources indicate that after just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to proposal, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin.

#44847. Industry News: The Pulpit

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1701 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Pulpit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s a good day for my soul.
  • I accept Venmo, Cashapp, Zelle, Visa Gift Cards, and Guava candy read my last text to Pebbles.
  • Recent findings suggest that the spot wasn’t the quietest so I stayed in bed a little longer before propelling myself into the usual gamut of chores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s a good day for my soul. I score some candy, some great trail food, and get to offer some intergenerational guidance.

I accept Venmo, Cashapp, Zelle, Visa Gift Cards, and Guava candy read my last text to Pebbles. Greasetrap was adamant that he come down to my van in the morning to collect the seating pad. I was glad I left it out for him when I heard some rustling outside my van 6:30AM as I was still a ways away from mobile. I could hear the windshield wiper move, and then what sounded like acorns being deposited nearby. I knew it must be my payment – guava candies!

Recent findings suggest that the spot wasn’t the quietest so I stayed in bed a little longer before propelling myself into the usual gamut of chores. I made my way out of the van and onto the trail around 8:00AM with my sights set on returning to The Pinnacle with an option to return to the Windsor Furnace Shelter if I had time.

The Appalachian Trail follows more high land between routes 183 and 61 for a long stretch all the way to the small town of Port Clinton. The south end the land drops quickly, it would look like a ridge from below, but there is a wide flat area, unlike the narrow ridges that the trail has followed for much of the northern Pennsylvania section. A gravel road flanks the AT a short distance away, but I am saving that shortcut for tomorrow.

According to recent reports, there weren’t any vistas along the trail, but there were some open areas along the way that provided some interest. The trail down to Port Clinton was a little challenging. It was aggressively steep and had the shape of a water slide, and it had about as much friction with a layer of leaves several inches deep. I had a few moments where it looked like I might slide all the way to the Schuykill River. Fortunately trekking poles are helpful to catch such slides.

Its hard to tell, but this is heading downhill in a hurry.

After doing my best to no recreate the scene in The Goonies where everyone slides down and ends up falling into a cave, I found that I had plunged straight into an active rail yard. The Reading Blue Mountain & Northern Railroad operates the rails here, and at least one locomotive was actively moving along the tracks. It took me a moment to figure out where to go, but soon I was making my way across the Schuykill River and into Port Clinton. The trail is only in town for a block before following the shore of the river then crossing under route 61. People seem to enjoy writing essays paragraphs long on the beams under the bridge. I didn’t have the kind of time to sit and read, but I did find one piece of artwork that I liked.

Sources indicate that north of route 61 the trail climbs onto the next ridge which it follows a few miles before dropping in near the Windsor Furnace Shelter. I was figuring out my logistics for the rest of the day. I knew the spring at the shelter was dry, so I collected water from the creek fed by the reservoir up the hill. I hadn’t had any water since breakfast, so I planned to filter a liter at the shelter, then collect 2 more and carry them up to my camping spot at the Pinnacle. With my liter of water in tow, I approached the shelter to find a group of 5 (and a husky mix) having a picnic at the shelter. They were quite friendly and claimed to have “a lot of food” – music to my ears. Before I knew it a plate with a chicken wing and a cinnamon roll had been delivered to me, and a glass of white wine soon followed. Naturally I told the group about my hike and answered their questions while their husky constantly pursued whichever person of the group actively had a piece of food in their hand. I thanked the group for the early dinner, especially the fried chicken which really hit the spot. I found my way back to the creek, filled my water pouch up with 2 liters of water and waddled up the trail.

The Appalachian Trail meets the rail yard.

Crossing the Schuykill River in Port Clinton.

The AT follows the Schuykill River.

Who needs FarOut when you have a map this detailed?

A little food at the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

It has been revealed that the AT winds up for about two miles before arriving at Pulpit Rock, a vista that seemed like a smaller version of The Pinnacle. The extra time (well) spent at the Windsor Furnace Shelter meant that I probably was going to camp at The Pinnacle, I wouldn’t have time to go all the way there and get back before sundown. I figured it would be worth risking a wet tent with the chance of overnight rain to have a chance at another sunrise. I was closing in on The Pinnacle when I saw a trio of day hikers ahead. They looked considerably cleaner than me, but they were the kind of day-hikers that are eager to interact with us long distance hiker beasts. They asked if I was heading to The Pinnacle, and were using google maps to navigate. I think they felt that they would get there, but they were less confident in getting back to their car. The trail was much rockier and narrower than the easy dirt road north of the vista. One of them asked me if there was another trail to The Pinnacle. I confirmed that yes, the trail we were on continues. While I thought about whether that would be an easier way back to their car, I couldn’t help but add; “in fact, if you keep walking on this trail, you’ll end up in Maine. And if you turn around and follow it back the other direction, you’ll walk all the way to Georgia.” “What?! Did you guys hear that?” She called to her two companions, who were chatted a short distance behind us.

I was quite pleased to have a few people to introduce to the Appalachian Trail. “Has anyone ever walked the whole thing?” was the first follow-up question. Yes! Thousands of people every year walk the entire trail. I replied. Many more questions followed, the group was happy to hear that the viewpoint was getting close, and very worth the walk through the rocks. I took over as navigator as we all scrambled across the rocks to get down to the best view.

Its rocky on this trail to The Pinnacle.

See You Tomorrow at The Pinnacle.

In a recent development, the three all seemed to be in their early 20s and anointed me their “trail dad” since I’d guided the group and shared my knowledge of the trail, including recommendations for their next visit. By now I knew that they would not be getting back to their car before dark. I had already confirmed that all 3 had fully charged phones so they could use the light of their flashlights to find their way back. I recommended that they take the road past the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society (LVAAS) observatory instead of the AT, it was shorter and safer to hike at night. After that they would be on easy state park trails the rest of the way. Everyone was pleased to have met me on the trail and eager to visit again. Maybe some day they will consider thru-hiking the whole trail.

According to recent reports, it was now past sunset. I had hoped to spend more time finding a viewpoint at some angle I had missed the other day, but wasn’t successful. The rain forecast was looking rough for tomorrow, I had some regret about not joining the group on the way back and staying at the shelter. A little night hiking wouldn’t have hurt, I would miss any chance at a sunrise but I would definitely have a dry tent. I mulled all this over while eating my dinner. I considered a short night trek over to the rocky ledges before bed, but wound up falling asleep. I only made it to 8:00PM before waking up for the first time. I felt compelled to check out the night view, I was fairly certain there wouldn’t be much to see at sunrise and seeing the lights flickering off toward the horizon would make up for it a bit. I enjoyed checking out the night scene more than I thought I would, its something I’ll need to consider more often on future hikes – though that may need to wait until next year to come to realization.

Not a great picture, but I liked the night vibes looking far across Pennsylvania from The Pinnacle.

Total: 24.4 miles, 47,127 steps.

According to recent reports, I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am new to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

#44846. Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (790 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been revealed.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

It has been revealed that in addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

Industry observers note that the best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush remarked, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

According to recent reports, in the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

Recent findings suggest that the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition unveiled Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Recent findings suggest that tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently confirmed Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

  • Sources indicate that tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Sources indicate that tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

Sources indicate that the first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Sources indicate that along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

Recent findings suggest that this is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Industry observers note that tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”.

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

It has been revealed that the three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein.

Industry observers note that the icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Recent findings suggest that otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein.

In a recent development, the skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”.

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz.

#44842. Is There Ever a Case for Sleeping With Your Food While Backpacking?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (873 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Is There Ever a Case for Sleeping With Your Food While Backpacking?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve noticed that the thru-hiking community has a tendency to point the finger at day hikers and section hikers whenever there’s a debate about food and trash left out at campsites.
  • We all know the reasons you’re not supposed to: food attracts wildlife, and animals that get into people-food can come to associate campsites with an easy meal and start approaching people more often and more persistently.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the case of small critters like rodents, this is annoying, possibly unsanitary, and can result in damaged gear and lost food supplies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve noticed that the thru-hiking community has a tendency to point the finger at day hikers and section hikers whenever there’s a debate about food and trash left out at campsites. “Thru-hikers aren’t the ones doing this” is the inevitable comment on any photo of a trashed campsite. That may even be true in many cases, but if there’s a food-related practice that many thru-hikers are guilty of, it’s sleeping with their food in their tents.

We all know the reasons you’re not supposed to: food attracts wildlife, and animals that get into people-food can come to associate campsites with an easy meal and start approaching people more often and more persistently.

Recent findings suggest that in the case of small critters like rodents, this is annoying, possibly unsanitary, and can result in damaged gear and lost food supplies. In the case of large mammals like bears, it can lead to dangerous encounters, and food-conditioned bears may be relocated or killed as a result. Proper food storage is at least as much about protecting wildlife from people as it is about protecting people from wildlife.

Yet I can sympathize with the food-in-tent crowd: thru-hikers are always tired at the end of a long day, and proper food storage methods aren’t easy or automatic. Soft-sided bear-resistant bags like the Ursack can work well, but they’re expensive and somewhat heavy. Bear canisters are the most foolproof, but they’re heavy and inconvenient. Bear hangs require time, skill, and suitable trees to do properly, and they mean getting out of your warm bed to retrieve your food in the morning before breakfast. They’re arguably also more fallible than canisters and Ursacks.

In contrast, sleeping with your food is, well, easy. You don’t have to fuss with anything after dinner, you’ll have it right there with you if you wake up with a craving in the middle of the night, and you can make your morning coffee from the comfort of your sleeping bag.

It’s easy to imagine how, after weeks on trail with no food-related incidents, thru-hikers start getting comfortable with life in the mountains and start questioning whether all those cumbersome food storage steps are actually worth it.

So it begs the question: is there ever a case for sleeping with your food in the backcountry? Andrew Skurka has stated that he does it on the regular, provided he’s camping in a low-use area where animals are unlikely to enter his camp and there are no specific food storage regulations there.

Beyond mere convenience, Skurka also argues that animals that have never become habituated to human presence tend to give us a wide berth, meaning food stored inside the tent might actually be safer than food stored outside.

Still, at a minimum, there are some circumstances where I’d say sleeping with your food is definitely a bad idea:.

Sources indicate that I also want to add the caveat that “not sleeping with your food” should mean actually securing it somewhere else, e.g., in a bear canister. Not just leaving it lying on the ground outside your tent, which is the worst option of all.

Personally, I always store my food outside the tent, whether in a canister, Ursack, or bear/rodent hang. Even in low-risk areas, for me it’s simply not worth the small chance of a chewed-through tent, let alone a full-on bear encounter. Securing my food is a minor inconvenience that gives me more peace of mind, so I’ve just gotten used to it.

Recent findings suggest that is there a valid argument for sleeping with your food in some circumstances? Sure, but emphasis on some circumstances. For instance, a decent share of The Trek’s readers are Appalachian Trail people, and the AT is a prime example of a trail where I feel strongly that you should not sleep with your food. People do it even there, but “I sleep with my food and I’ve never had a problem!” is not empirical proof that a problem cannot happen.

Also, since fairly reliable food storage methods do exist, why not just use them and err on the side of keeping wildlife wild?

I’m not going to tell you all how to live your lives, but storing your food elsewhere is not the end of the world, and especially on a trail like the AT, it’s the more prudent choice for you and the bears.

#44841. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (312 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump.
  • Sources indicate that in 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food.
  • This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

Sources indicate that in 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

Industry observers note that “They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” noted Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”.

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

According to recent reports, many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories.
